See also: [LVMH](/wiki/LVMH "LVMH")

He worked with Alain Chevalier, CEO of Moët Hennessy, and [Henry Racamier](/wiki/Henry_Racamier "Henry Racamier"), president of [Louis Vuitton](/wiki/Louis_Vuitton "Louis Vuitton"), to form LVMH in 1987.[[17]](#cite_note-18)

In July 1988, Arnault provided $1.6 billion to form a holding company with [Guinness](/wiki/Guinness "Guinness") that held 24% of LVMH's shares. In response to rumors that the Louis Vuitton group was buying LVMH's stock to form a "blocking minority", Arnault spent $600 million to buy 13.5% more of LVMH, making him LVMH's largest shareholder. LVMH had been created on the premise that the conglomerate would be too large for a single hostile raider.[[15]](#cite_note-:0-16) However, the premise failed to take into account internal takeover attempts. The fault became too large to ignore when Arnault had a differing strategic vision from Racamier, Louis Vuitton's president.[[18]](#cite_note-:2-19)

In January 1989, he spent another $500 million to gain control of a total of 43.5% of LVMH's shares and 35% of its voting rights, thus reaching the "blocking minority" that he needed to stop the dismantlement of the LVMH group.[[18]](#cite_note-:2-19) He then turned on Racamier, stripped him of his power, and ousted him from the board of directors.[[15]](#cite_note-:0-16) On 13 January 1989, he was unanimously elected chairman of the executive management board.[[18]](#cite_note-:2-19)

New interface elements were integrated, including sheets ([dialog boxes](/wiki/Dialog_box "Dialog box") attached to specific windows) and drawers, which would slide out and provide options.

The use of soft edges, translucent colors, and pinstripes, similar to the hardware design of the first [iMacs](/wiki/IMac "IMac"), brought more texture and color to the user interface when compared to what [Mac OS 9](/wiki/Mac_OS_9 "Mac OS 9") and [Mac OS X Server 1.0](/wiki/Mac_OS_X_Server_1.0 "Mac OS X Server 1.0")'s [Platinum](/wiki/Platinum_(theme) "Platinum (theme)") appearance had offered. State and regional [cancer registries](/wiki/Cancer_registry "Cancer registry") are organizations that abstract clinical data about cancer from patient medical records. These institutions provide information to state and national public health groups to help track trends in cancer diagnosis and treatment. One of the largest and most important [cancer registries](/wiki/Cancer_registry "Cancer registry") is [Surveillance Epidemiology and End Results](/wiki/Surveillance_Epidemiology_and_End_Results "Surveillance Epidemiology and End Results") (SEER), administered by the [US Federal government](/wiki/US_Federal_government "US Federal government").[[5]](#cite_note-5)

Health information privacy concerns have led to the restricted use of [cancer registry](/wiki/Cancer_registry "Cancer registry") data in the [United States Department of Veterans Affairs](/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Veterans_Affairs "United States Department of Veterans Affairs")[[6]](#cite_note-lancetva-6)[[7]](#cite_note-mpva-7)[[8]](#cite_note-nytva-8) and other institutions.[[9]](#cite_note-iomhip-9) The American Cancer Society predicts that approximately 1,690,000 new cancer cases will be diagnosed and 577,000 Americans will ultimately die of cancer in 2012.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

[Observational epidemiological studies](/wiki/Observational_study "Observational study") that show associations between risk factors and specific cancers mostly serve to generate hypotheses about potential interventions that could reduce cancer incidence or [morbidity](/wiki/Morbidity "Morbidity"). [Randomized controlled trials](/wiki/Randomized_controlled_trial "Randomized controlled trial") then test whether hypotheses generated by epidemiological studies and laboratory research actually result in reduced cancer incidence and mortality. In many cases, findings from observational [epidemiological](/wiki/Epidemiological "Epidemiological") studies are not confirmed by randomized controlled trials.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

Lucas initially planned to use pre-existing music for *Star Wars*, rather than an original score. Since the film portrayed alien worlds, he believed recognizable music was needed to create a sense of familiarity. He hired [John Williams](/wiki/John_Williams "John Williams") as a music consultant, and showed him a collection of orchestral pieces he intended to use for the soundtrack.[[202]](#cite_note-222) After Williams convinced Lucas that an original score would be preferable, Lucas tasked him with creating it. A few of the composer's finished pieces were influenced by Lucas' initial orchestral selections. The "Main Title Theme" was inspired by the theme from the 1942 film *[Kings Row](/wiki/Kings_Row "Kings Row")*, scored by [Erich Wolfgang Korngold](/wiki/Erich_Wolfgang_Korngold "Erich Wolfgang Korngold"), and the "Dune Sea of Tatooine" was influenced by the music of the 1948 film *[Bicycle Thieves](/wiki/Bicycle_Thieves "Bicycle Thieves")*, scored by [Alessandro Cicognini](/wiki/Alessandro_Cicognini "Alessandro Cicognini"). Lucas later denied he ever considered using pre-existing music for the film.[[203]](#cite_note-223)[[204]](#cite_note-224)

Over a period of 12 days in March 1977, Williams and the [London Symphony Orchestra](/wiki/London_Symphony_Orchestra "London Symphony Orchestra") recorded the *Star Wars* score.[[69]](#cite_note-Dreams-77) The soundtrack was released as a double LP in 1977 by [20th Century Fox Records](/wiki/20th_Century_Fox_Records "20th Century Fox Records").[[205]](#cite_note-225)[[206]](#cite_note-226) In 2005, the [American Film Institute](/wiki/American_Film_Institute "American Film Institute") chose the *Star Wars* soundtrack as the best film score of all time.[[207]](#cite_note-AFIscore-227)

Venus is the second planet from the Sun, making a full orbit in about 224 days.

Venus orbits the Sun at an average distance of about 0.72 [AU](/wiki/Astronomical_unit "Astronomical unit") (108 million [km](/wiki/Kilometre "Kilometre"); 67 million [mi](/wiki/Mile "Mile")), and completes an orbit every 224.7 days. It completes 13 orbits in 7.998 years, so its position in our sky almost repeats every eight years. Although all planetary [orbits](/wiki/Orbit "Orbit") are [elliptical](/wiki/Ellipse "Ellipse"), Venus's orbit is currently the closest to circular, with an [eccentricity](/wiki/Orbital_eccentricity "Orbital eccentricity") of less than 0.01.[[6]](#cite_note-fact-6) Simulations of the early solar system orbital dynamics have shown that the eccentricity of the Venus orbit may have been substantially larger in the past, reaching values as high as 0.31 and possibly impacting early climate evolution.[[142]](#cite_note-psj_1_42-144)
